title: Creature Habitat
goal: Your kid invents an animal that has never existed, works out exactly how it stays alive, builds it with their hands and creates the habitat where it thrives. Then they document it like a scientist who just discovered a new species. Every feature has to earn its place.
need: Paper and markers or coloured pencils
Clay or playdough, cardboard, small boxes, tape, glue and scissors
Natural materials if you're outside: sticks, leaves, rocks, bark, mud
Fabric scraps, pipe cleaners or foil (optional)

lesson.text: Every body part a real animal has does a job. An invented creature works the same way: if a feature can't answer 'how does this help it survive?', it doesn't belong.
lesson.before: My creature has wings, horns, fur, gills and laser eyes.

model.line: It lives in the desert. Huge ears let body heat out, like a fennec fox's.
They warn predators it's poisonous, like a poison dart frog's bright colours.
It can't see well at night, so owls are its biggest danger.
Every feature has a job, and the creature has a weakness too.

lesson.modelNote: The first try was a pile of cool parts. The fix keeps fewer features, gives each one a job and adds a weakness, the way real animals work.

howTo.intro: Your best tool here is one question: 'how does that help it survive?' If they want a flying fish with fur, let them, then ask it. Resist fixing the build. 'Tell me about this part' beats 'maybe try it this way.'

plan.what: Invent the creature and design how it survives (Steps 1 and 2).
Build the creature and its habitat (Steps 3 and 4).
Make the field guide page and reveal the discovery (Step 5). It also works as one long afternoon.

troubleshoot.q: They want to draw a dragon or a unicorn
troubleshoot.a: Fine as a start. Ask 'what makes yours different from every other dragon?' and let the survival questions do the rest.

troubleshoot.q: They don't want to make the field guide
troubleshoot.a: Let it go, or let them dictate while you write. The learning is in the inventing and building.

skills.name: Making
skills.text: turning a sketch into something solid

steps.title: Invent your creature
steps.why: The name and personality shape every choice that follows.
steps.kid: Your kid sketches an animal that has never existed. They decide what it's covered in (scales, feathers, fur, skin), how big it is and what colour, and why. Then they name it and give it a personality: shy, fierce, goofy.
steps.you: Ask questions that push their thinking without steering it. If they start from a dragon or a unicorn, ask what makes theirs different.
ask: What's the first thing someone would notice about it?
Where did the idea for this animal come from?
steps.tip: Real animals are the best idea bank. Mix two, like half owl and half octopus, then make it their own.

levels.explore: Draw the creature and give it a name.
levels.develop: Draw it, name it, and explain its colour and covering.
levels.extend: Draw it to scale next to a real animal of the same size, and decide what that size means for how much it eats and where it can hide.

steps.title: Design how it survives
steps.kid: Your kid works out what the creature eats and how it finds food, how it defends itself when something bigger shows up, and what its weakness is. They use the Real animal tricks card in the Creature Lab Toolkit at the end of the guide for ideas, and give every feature a reason.
steps.you: Push them to connect each feature to a purpose. If they're stuck, flip it: pick a danger first, then design the body part that handles it.
ask: If it went a whole day without eating, what would happen?
What is your creature most afraid of?
steps.tip: No invincible creatures. Even the toughest real animals have something that threatens them.

levels.explore: Draw what it eats and one way it stays safe.
levels.develop: Give every feature a job, and name its weakness.
levels.extend: Give each feature a cost as well as a job. Huge ears let heat out in the desert but would lose too much in the Arctic, which is why arctic foxes have small ears. Name the cost of each feature.

steps.title: Build the creature
steps.why: From a sketch to something they can hold.
steps.kid: Your kid builds their creature: a detailed drawing, a clay sculpture or a cardboard and craft-supply model. First they pick which features matter most, since they probably can't build every detail.
steps.you: Help with tricky construction moments, but keep your hands off the creative choices. If it falls apart, that's a problem to solve together.
ask: Which feature was hardest to build, and how did you solve it?
What would you change if you built it again?
steps.tip: A lopsided clay creature they built themselves teaches more than a perfect one you shaped.

levels.explore: Build the creature from clay, paper or cardboard.
levels.develop: Build it with its most important survival features showing.
levels.extend: Build it so it stands on its own, and make one part move or open.

steps.title: Build its habitat
steps.why: The home has to match the body.
steps.kid: Your kid decides exactly where their creature lives, not just 'forest' but a dark cave with underground rivers or a windy cliff covered in moss. They check it against the Habitat match card, then build it in a shoebox or outside in a real spot.
steps.you: Connect their habitat to the features they designed: thick white fur doesn't make sense on a tropical beach.
ask: What's the most dangerous part of this habitat for your creature?
What would happen if the weather changed a lot?
steps.tip: A shoebox world full of details beats a big empty one. Paint the inside, add paper trees, use sand or soil for the ground.

levels.explore: Build a habitat with a place to sleep, eat and hide.
levels.develop: Build a habitat that matches every survival feature.
levels.extend: Add a food chain: a plant at the bottom, what your creature eats, and what eats it.

steps.title: Make the field guide and reveal it
steps.why: Scientists document a discovery, then share it.
steps.kid: Your kid makes a field guide page as if they just discovered a new species, using the Field guide checklist card. Then they set the creature in its habitat and present it to someone: what it is, how it survives, why it lives there.
steps.you: Be a curious audience. Ask real questions, not quiz questions.
ask: Would another scientist have enough to identify it?
What if two of these creatures competed for the same food?
steps.tip: Don't worry about spelling. Younger kids can dictate while you write, or just draw and label.

levels.explore: Draw and label it, then show it to someone.
levels.develop: Fill in every part of the checklist and present it.
levels.extend: Give it a two-part scientific name, like Vulpes zerda for the fennec fox, and add a 'not to be confused with' line saying how to tell it from a real animal.

reference.title: Creature Lab Toolkit
reference.intro: Tricks real animals use, what body parts are for, how to match a home, and what goes in a field guide.

lines.v: giant ears let off heat in the desert
a white winter coat hides it in snow
its hump stores fat, not water

items.name: Body part jobs

lines.v: hear danger or prey, or let off heat
see all around, common in prey

items.ask: Does every feature have a job?

items.name: Habitat match

lines.v: thick fur or a layer of fat
big ears, stored fat, active at night

items.ask: Does your creature fit its home?

items.name: Field guide checklist

lines.v: what it eats, and how it finds it

items.ask: Could someone identify it from your page?

after.label: Creature rules
lines: It eats something, and something eats it.

conclusion.headline: A new species, discovered.
conclusion.text: Point to any part of their creature and ask what it's for. They'll have an answer, and a weakness to go with it. Expect the same question about real animals on your next walk.
conclusion.celebrate: Name the one feature that convinced you, and say why in a sentence: 'The webbed feet make sense. It lives where the river floods.'
extensions: Invent a second creature for the same habitat and work out how the two get along
Write a short story starring the creature
Compare their habitat with a real ecosystem
Make a whole field guide, one page per creature

signs: They ask 'what is that for?' about real animals
They notice camouflage and warning colours outside
They explain choices with a reason, not just 'because it's cool'
makeItReal: At the zoo, on a walk or during a documentary, ask them to spot one feature and guess its job. Then look it up together and see who was right.
levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.
cta: Want the next one? This guide is one of 120+ in the Anywhere Learning library, each with your job and your kid's job at every step.
